Definition
The JK flip-flop is the most common and versatile of the flip-flop family.
INTRODUCTIONM
It can be used in any flip-flop or latch application by configuring its inputs for the desired function..d function.

LESSON MENU
The JK flip-flop is designed to store its last input conditions until the next input conditions are applied.
DISCUSSION
JK flip-flops have five inputs and two outputs...............
"CLK" is a label used to denote the clock input. You may also see the clock input labeled as CK, C and CP.P.P.nd CP...are also used to indicate the clock input..
Like a traffic light synchronizes the movement of vehicles at an intersection, the clock of a flip-flop is used to synchronize the transfer of data through the flip-flop. synchronous input.
Clocking for the JK flip-flop is most often negative edge triggered, but positive edge triggered JK flip-flops are also common.

Internally, the JK flip-flop is more complex than many of the other flip-flops and latches. Analyzing ("bit chasing") the circuit from a gate level would be time consuming and confusing. Gate level analysis will not be performed in this lesson.
While the JK's behavior exhibits properties of other flip- flops, it is unique. Let's examine the truth table.

As with the D Flip-Flop, the PRESET and CLEAR inputs will override any other input conditions on the flip-flop. Regardless of the operation taking place, an activated Preset or Clear will either Set or Reset the flip-flop. The truth table indicates this through the use of asterisks (*))ks (*)))

As with the D Flip-Flop, the PRESET and CLEAR inputs will override any other input conditions on the flip-flop. Regardless of the operation taking place, an activated Preset or Clear will either Set or Reset the flip-flop. The truth table indicates this through the use of asterisks (*)sks (*)))
DEFINITION
PRESET - A condition where a flip-flop's outputs have Q high and Q low. This condition may be considered as: Preset =Set.
DEFINITION
CLEAR - A condition where a flip-flop's outputs have Q low and Q high. This condition may be considered as: Clear =Reset.

In this example, the Preset and Clear inputs are active low. This means that a low applied to either the Preset or Clear lines will place the Q and Q outputs in a Set or Reset condition, respectively...

Just as you would not try to turn on and turn off a light at the same time, neither would you want to try to Preset and Clear a flip-flop simultaneously. Aside from not serving any purpose, the flip-flop will go into a race condition.escribed in the RS Latch lesson.
Some JK flip-flops are manufactured so that the Preset and Clear lines are active high. In that case, the symbol and truth table is changed to reflect the difference as shown below.
When a Preset or Clear line is tied to its inactive state, the outputs are not affected; the input is effectively removed from the circuit. This allows the synchronous inputs to be used...

One last word on the Preset and Clear inputs: If the inputs are not going to be used by the circuit, the lines should be tied to their inactive state. This will prevent the lines from floating to their active condition or allow noise to be introduced into the circuit...

The J and K inputs of the flip-flop are clock dependent. That is, no data on these inputs will be processed by the flip-flop unless the clock input has been satisfied. These are called synchronous inputs...

The J and K inputs of the flip-flop are clock dependent. That is, no data on these inputs will be processed by the flip-flop unless the clock input has been satisfied. These are called synchronous inputs...
DEFINITION
SYNCHRONOUS - Having a fixed time relationship. The output of a device changes state only at a specified point on a triggering input, such as a clock signal.

The exception to this is the first JK input condition shown in the truth table: J = 0, K = 0. This is a NO CHANGE condition, sometimes represented in truth tables as HOLD. The clock may be pulsed, but nothing will occur at the outputs...
The behavior of the JK flip-flop for the next two input conditions is identical to the RS Flip-Flop.
If J=0 and K=1 when the negative edge of the clock pulse is applied, the Q output will go low and the Q output will go high. The flip-flop will be in a Reset condition..
Conversely, if J=1 and K=0 when the negative edge of the clock pulse is applied, the Q output will go high and the Q will go low. The flip-flop will be in the Set condition..
The final input possibility to be considered is when J and K are both high. It is this condition that makes the JK flip-flop so important and unique.
The truth table shows that under the J=1, K=1 condition, the Q and Q outputs will reverse from whatever condition they were in prior to the clock pulse..
For as long as the J and K inputs are held high, every time the clock input is pulsed, the outputs will reverse.
The toggle condition of the JK flip-flop is extremely useful in the construction of registers and counters...

The "toggle" condition can be created in other flip-flops by cross-connecting their outputs to their opposing input(s).
In the first example, an RS Flip-Flop has been wired in such a way that the Q output is fed back to the R input and the Q output is connected to the S input.. and Q output line HG))
If we assume the following input conditions, everytime the clock pulse is applied, the outputs load their logic levels on opposing inputs.

The same operation can be realized with the D Flip-Flop. The Q output is cross-connected to the D input. Since normal operation forces Q to whatever logic level was on D at the time of the clock pulse, Q will always be the opposite of D....
In theory, the JK flip-flop can be constructed to operate with level triggering. That is, the clock input is either held high or held low for its active state.

The flip-flop would behave normally until the toggle condition was applied to the inputs. Ultimately, in such a case, the Q and Q outputs would begin to oscillate at an uncontrolled rate (likely in the GHz range) based solely on the propagation delay of the gates....
Since the outputs would not be controllable, level triggered JK flip-flops are not manufactured.constructed.

Since the Preset and Clear lines override the inputs, they should be examined first.
Looking first at the Preset signal, we can see that the flip-flop's Q output will go high about mid-way through T1 and then again during the latter part of T3.

Even though the pulses are of short duration, the Q and Q outputs will remain in a Set condition until they are changed either by a Clear signal or by the synchronous inputs J and K.K.s inputs J and K.. inputs J and K.
The Clear line is activated only once, between T2 and T3. This places the Q and Q outputs in a Reset (Clear) state..
Just as with Preset, the Clear condition will remain in effect at the outputs after the pulse, until the flip-flop is either Preset or changed by conditions at the synchronous inputs.
Since the J and K inputs can only affect the outputs at the time of the positive edge of the clock, we need only look at the condition of J and K at that time..
At T1, the J input is low and the K input is high. Under these conditions the flip-flop will Reset, making Q low. Q will remain low until the Preset pulse..........ontinue until the Preset pulse..
At T2, the J input is high and the K input is low. This means Q will remain at a logic high.
Between T2 and T3, the Clear pulse comes in, driving Q low again. Q will remain low until T3.
A toggle condition is present at T3 because both J and K are high. Since (at this time) Q is low, it will be driven high by the toggle. Q will remain high until T4...
At T4, J is low and K is high. This means that Q will drop to a logic low. With no Preset pulses remaining, Q will remain low until T5.
Finally, at T5, J is high and K is low. Again, Q must go high.
The outputs of a JK flip-flop are always the compliment of each other. Therefore the Q output is a mirror image of the Q output.

JK flip-flops are sometimes manufactured with multiple J and multiple K inputs. These flip-flops are nothing more than typical JK flip-flops whose J and K inputs are fed by AND gates. A triple input JK flip-flop is depicted below....
Functionally, multiple input flip-flops operate the same. The only difference is that in order to place a high on the J or K inputs, all legs of the desired AND gate must be high at the same time.

Examine the inputs to the flip-flop below. Preset and Clear have been disabled. J1, J2 and J3 are 1,0,1 and K1, K2 and K3 are 1,1,1. This means that the J input is receiving a low and the K input is receiving a high. With the clock satisfied, Q will go low and Q will go high....
Timing diagrams for multiple input JK flip-flops are a bit more complex due to the additional input lines. Still, a methodical, attentive approach will make calculating the outputs less of a trauma.

Just as before, look first at the Preset and Clear. The flip-flop is cleared (reset) beginning just past T3. Since the pulse extends past T4, Q will be low from the start of the pulse till at least T5.
A Preset pulse comes in between T5 and T6. This will keep Q high until at least T6.
Moving to T1, J1, J2 and J3 are high. This puts a high on J. K1 is low, so the signals on K2 and K3 are irrelevant; K must be low. With this input condition, Q goes high.
At T2, all three J inputs are high and K1 is low. This means that Q will continue to be high.
A NO CHANGE condition occurs at T3 because J2 and K1 are low, keeping the outputs of both AND gates low. This keeps Q in a high state.

As we have already established, between T3 and T4 the Clear pulse comes in and so Q goes low. Since the Clear pulse continues past the negative edge of the clock at T4, the TOGGLE condition at the J and K inputs is ignored. Q remains low.
Between T5 and T6, a Preset pulse occurs, which drives Q to a high state.
At T6, J1 and J3 are low while all the K inputs are high. This input condition drives Q to a low state.
Since J3 is low, and the rest of the inputs are high, the same condition exists at T7 that existed at T6. Q stays low.
At T8, all the J inputs and all the K inputs are high, creating a TOGGLE condition. This drives Q to a high state.
Finally, at T9, J2 is low while all other inputs are high. This puts Q in a low condition.
